name: The Antechamber
description: A stone room with three doors. Torchlight. The air is still and old. Above each door, words are carved into the lintel — poems worn smooth by time but still legible. This is a threshold. What comes next depends on you.

layers.note: irregular popping, the fat in the beeswax igniting
amplified by the dome — you hear yourself from above
low hum, barely audible, air moving in a space beyond

surface_textures: flagstone underfoot — cold, uneven, worn into shallow valleys by centuries of feet
stone walls — rough-hewn blocks with mortar lines you can trace with your fingertips
iron torch brackets — cold enough to sting, bolted deep into the wall
carved stone lintels above each door — smooth where hands have touched them, sharp where the chisel cut
touch.air_feel: Still. Cool. The air has weight to it — not damp exactly, but dense. It has been in this room for a long time. The torches consume oxygen and replace it with carbon, and you can feel that in the slight thickness of each breath.
touch.thermal_notes: Stone walls at 10°C radiate cold — you feel it before you touch them, the infrared deficit pulling heat from exposed skin. The torches create a narrow cone of radiant warmth (800°C flame surface, but it drops to background by two meters). Standing between torches, you are cold. Standing near one, one side of your face is warm and the other is not.
key_tactile_moments: Running your fingers over the carved poems — the letters are grooved 3mm deep, and your fingertips read them faster than your eyes in this light
The door handles — iron rings, cold, heavy, they resist before they turn
The flagstone under bare feet — the cold is immediate and total, limestone conducting heat away at 1.7 W/m·K

cross_sensory_bridges: Torchlight and torch-smoke are the same event — combustion producing both the light you see by and the carbon you smell. The room is illuminated by its own burning.

The cold of the stone and the cold of the iron are different temperatures at the same temperature — iron at 10°C feels colder than stone at 10°C because it conducts heat 30x faster. Your hand knows which door frame is stone and which is iron without looking.
The silence has texture — the stone walls reflect sound so efficiently that the absence of sound becomes a presence. You hear the room's shape in what it doesn't say.

shared_causes.effects: The walls create the cold (thermal mass), the acoustics (hard reflection), the smell (mineral off-gas), and the visual texture (grey, rough, ancient). One material, four senses, all saying the same thing: you are underground, in something old, and it will outlast you.

The torches create the light (orange, flickering, 1800K), the warmth (radiant, directional, limited), the smell (smoke, beeswax, carbon), and the sound (crackle, hiss). The room exists because something is burning in it.

positions.name: the threshold
positions.description: You have just entered. The room opens before you — circular, domed, three doors evenly spaced in the far wall. Two torches flank each door. The floor is a single slab of limestone, cracked once down the center.
positions.smell_notes: Stone-dominant. The torch smoke rises and pools at the dome's apex — you smell it less at floor level, more when you look up. Cedar from the torch handles.
positions.sight_notes: Six torches. Orange light, hard shadows. The dome catches the light and curves it — the ceiling glows while the floor stays dark. The three doors are identical in size but different in wood: dark oak, pale ash, red-brown mahogany.
positions.sound_notes: Your own breathing. The torches hissing. A faint draft from under one of the doors — air moving somewhere beyond them. The dome creates a subtle resonance; sounds made here come back to you a half-second later, softened.
positions.touch_notes: Cold floor through your feet. Still air on your face. The radiant warmth of the nearest torch on your right cheek.
positions.cross_sensory: The dome is a lens for all senses — it focuses sound back to center, pools smoke at its peak, and bounces torchlight into a diffuse orange glow. The architecture shapes every sense simultaneously.

positions.name: before the three doors
positions.description: You stand equidistant from all three doors. Above each, carved into the stone lintel, is a poem. The carvings are old — centuries, maybe more — but maintained. Someone has been keeping these words legible.
positions.smell_notes: Each door leaks a different scent. The dark oak door: cold mineral air, water. The pale ash door: thin clean wind, altitude. The mahogany door: woodsmoke, warmth, bread.
positions.sight_notes: The poems are visible in the torchlight. The letters cast tiny shadows in their grooves. Each door has a different grain — the oak is dense and dark, the ash is light with visible rings, the mahogany has a red depth that swallows the torchlight.
positions.sound_notes: The draft is clearer here. The dark oak door: a faint dripping echo. The pale ash door: wind, distant but real. The mahogany door: silence, but a warm silence — the kind that has people in it somewhere.
positions.touch_notes: If you place your palm flat on each door, the oak is cold and damp. The ash is cold and dry. The mahogany is faintly warm — there is heat beyond it.
positions.cross_sensory: Each door is a preview. The senses leak through the wood and the gaps beneath, and each door tells a different story about what waits beyond. You can choose with your eyes, your nose, your ears, or your hands. They all agree.

light.note: 1800K is candlelight orange. The dome diffuses it upward — ceiling glows, floor stays dark. Shadows are soft-edged and move with the flame.

impossible_detail: Iron at 10°C conducts heat at 80 W/m·K. Limestone at 10°C conducts at 1.3 W/m·K. Same temperature, same room — but touch the iron door hinge and your hand recoils. Touch the stone wall and the cold seeps in slowly. Your skin doesn't measure temperature. It measures heat flux — how fast energy leaves your body. The iron is stealing from you 60 times faster.
